heard: 25 million space rocks slam into Earth's atmosphere every single day. We call these bright flashes shooting stars, but they are not distant stars at all. While drifting through deep space, a tiny rock fragment is known as a meteoroid. The moment it plunges into our atmosphere and ignites, it becomes a fiery meteor. Major showers like August's Perseids happen when Earth plows directly through dusty comet trails. Most meteoroids vaporize completely, but any surviving piece that hits the surface becomes a meteorite. Surprisingly, some of these retrieved meteorites are actual pieces of planetary— debris blasted off Mars or the Moon.
